title: Checking the Answer
intro: Learn a four-step habit for checking an AI answer: spot, ask, cross-check and decide, and when to ask a qualified person.
recap: Names, numbers, dates, quotes and links are the parts most likely to be wrong.
Spot the risky parts, ask for its basis, cross-check elsewhere, then decide what to use.
Do not use the same chatbot to confirm its own answer.
For health, law or money, also ask a qualified person.

aiTutor.recap: Chatbots can sound sure while being wrong, so anything that matters needs a second check. The checking is not about distrusting the tool; it is about not passing on a mistake.
aiTutor.example: Kemi puts the chatbot's statistic and the report's name on her slide. A classmate searches for the report and cannot find it. She has to correct the slide in front of everyone.
aiTutor.watchOut: A source with a real-sounding title, a year and an author can still be invented. Looking real is not the same as being real.
aiTutor.tryThis: The next time a chatbot gives you a number or a name, spend one minute searching for it somewhere else.

glossary.definition: A number that describes something, such as a percentage or a count. Chatbots can invent statistics that look precise.
glossary.example: "73% of students prefer online lessons" is a statistic. It needs a real source before you use it.

glossary.definition: Words someone is said to have written or spoken. Chatbots sometimes give a quote that the person never said.
glossary.example: A famous line attributed to a well-known leader may actually come from someone else, or from nobody.

paragraphs: Made-up story: Kemi asks a chatbot for a statistic for her school presentation. It gives a precise number and the name of a report. She puts both on her slide. Later she finds that the report does not exist.

The chatbot did not lie on purpose. It wrote text that looked like a real fact. Names, numbers, dates, quotes and web links are the things it gets wrong most easily, because they must be exactly right.
The habit is simple: use the answer as a starting point, and check the parts that matter before you rely on them or share them.

aiTutor.explain: Tap each step. You do not need all four every time, but the more it matters, the more of them you do. The steps run in a loop you can repeat for anything important.
aiTutor.example: A chatbot says a new law starts in March. You spot the date, ask where it is from, look it up on an official government site, and keep only what the official page confirms.
aiTutor.watchOut: Asking the chatbot "Are you sure?" does not count as a check. It may repeat the same error with new confidence.
aiTutor.tryThis: Choose one fact from a recent chatbot answer and take it through the four steps.

walkThrough.title: Checking a chatbot's claim: "A new rule starts in March."
steps: Spot: the date and the rule are exact facts, so they are the parts to check.
Ask: you ask where it comes from. It names an official-sounding source. That is a clue, not proof.
Cross-check: you search for the rule on an official government website, not through the chatbot.
Decide: the official page says the rule starts in June. You use June and leave out the chatbot's date.
Result: you caught a mistake in two minutes, before you passed it on.

nodes.label: 1. Spot
nodes.title: Spot the risky parts
nodes.definition: Mark the exact facts: names, numbers, dates, quotes, links and any advice with real consequences. These are the parts to check.
nodes.bonusFact: General explanations are usually safer than precise facts.

nodes.label: 2. Ask
nodes.title: Ask it to show its basis
nodes.definition: Ask "How sure are you?" or "What source is this from?". The answer is a clue, not proof, because it can invent sources too.
nodes.bonusFact: A source you cannot find yourself is a warning sign.

nodes.label: 3. Cross-check
nodes.title: Cross-check elsewhere
nodes.definition: Look the fact up in a separate, reliable place: an official website, a trusted news outlet, a textbook, or an expert. Two independent sources that agree are better than one.
nodes.bonusFact: Do not use the same chatbot to confirm its own answer.

nodes.label: 4. Decide
nodes.title: Decide what to use
nodes.definition: Keep what you confirmed, fix what is wrong, and leave out anything you could not check. For health, law or money, also ask a qualified person.
nodes.bonusFact: Leaving out an unchecked fact is better than sharing a wrong one.

widgetData.completionMessage: You have the four steps: spot, ask, cross-check, decide.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: The more a mistake would cost, the more steps you should take. A casual fact needs a glance; a medicine dose needs a pharmacist.

aiTutor.explain: Look for the exact, checkable fact. Tone and layout cannot be wrong in a way that hurts you, but a date, a name or a number can be.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not check the parts that are easy to check. Check the parts that would do the most damage if they were wrong.

widgetData.question: A chatbot writes a paragraph about a famous event. Which part should you check first?
widgetData.explanation: Exact facts are where a polished-looking answer is most often wrong, and where a mistake does the most damage when you pass it on.
widgetData.bonusFact: A quick search for one key name or number often reveals whether the whole answer is solid. If the main fact fails, treat the rest with care.

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false. Think about who or what is a separate, reliable source, and which sources only repeat the chatbot's answer.
aiTutor.tryThis: For each card, name one place you could check the claim yourself.

widgetData.instruction: Is each statement true or false?

cards.statement: A source or web link given by a chatbot is real because it looks proper.
cards.explanation: Chatbots can invent sources and links. Open the link, or search for the source yourself.
cards.bonusFact: Search for the source's name yourself. If you cannot find it, do not use it.

cards.statement: Asking the same chatbot "Are you sure?" is a full check.
cards.explanation: It may repeat or change its answer without checking anything. Use a separate source.
cards.bonusFact: Use a different, reliable place for the check, not the chatbot that wrote the answer.

cards.statement: For health, law or money decisions, a chatbot answer should be checked with a qualified person.
cards.explanation: A wrong answer here can cost you a lot, so it is worth a second, expert opinion.
cards.bonusFact: A pharmacist, doctor, lawyer or adviser can confirm what a chatbot may only have guessed.

cards.statement: If two independent trusted sources agree with the answer, you can feel more confident.
cards.explanation: Independent agreement is the best everyday check you have.
cards.bonusFact: Two sources that found their facts separately and agree are much stronger than one.

aiTutor.review: Match each claim to a good way to check it. The best check is a separate, reliable source, such as an official website, a pharmacist or a trusted book.
aiTutor.example: A quote attributed to a famous person: search for the exact words together with the person's name, and see if a trusted site or book gives the same source.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not use a link the chatbot gave you as your only proof. Open it, and check that the page exists and says what the chatbot claimed.

widgetData.instruction: Match each claim to a good way to check it:

pairs.right: Find it on the official source's own site

pairs.left: A quote from a famous person
pairs.right: Search for the quote in a trusted book or site

pairs.left: A web link it gave you
pairs.right: Open it and see if the page exists
Ask a pharmacist or a doctor

widgetData.explanation: Each check uses a separate, reliable source rather than the chatbot itself.

aiTutor.review: Finish the habit sentence. It is the shortest form of everything in this lesson.
aiTutor.tryThis: Say the sentence to yourself the next time you are about to share something a chatbot told you.

widgetData.template: Use the chatbot answer as a starting point, and {blank} anything important before you share it.
widgetData.explanation: Verifying is the step that turns a quick draft into something you can stand behind. It takes a few minutes and protects your reputation.
widgetData.bonusFact: Saying "I checked this" is more convincing than "the AI said so". People trust what you can show, not what a tool told you.
